tagline: Four freeway lanes past forests and towns shaped by anthracite mining
intro: The Governor Casey Byway follows a four-lane freeway between Carbondale Township and Dunmore, with forested stretches beside Lackawanna County's developed communities. The Moosic Mountains lie east of the highway. PennDOT records the Pennsylvania Byway designation as effective January 6, 2004. VisitPA highlights access to Steamtown National Historic Site, the Pennsylvania Anthracite Heritage Museum and the Lackawanna Coal Mine.

U.S. 6 did not always reach Carbondale through Scranton. The 1926 route used roads now numbered Pennsylvania 706, U.S. 11 and Pennsylvania 106 between Wyalusing and Carbondale. By the end of 1927 it had exchanged routes with U.S. 106, taking the southern route through Scranton. The modern freeway bypasses Carbondale to the east, while Business Route 6 runs through town on Main Street. The byway designation came under Act 33 of 2003.

Begin at the Business Route 6 junction in Carbondale Township and follow westbound U.S. 6 toward Dunmore. The Carbondale bypass has a westbound scenic overlook. Continue past the interchanges serving Jermyn and Mayfield, Archbald, Jessup and Olyphant. Near Throop, the highway passes between a landfill and the forested Moosic Mountains. Wooded sections lead toward developed areas and the I-81 junction in Dunmore.

moments.title: Carbondale
moments.text: Carbondale grew with anthracite mining on land developed by William and Maurice Wurts, founders of the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company. The Delaware and Hudson Gravity Railroad began operating between Carbondale and Honesdale in 1829. The railroad's gravity shops have been demolished. The city's history is kept at the Carbondale Historical Society and Museum, on the municipal building's third floor. Built in 1892–1894, that brick-and-bluestone building incorporates an older, 1859 courthouse wing and has a five-story corner tower. Its Romanesque design includes a large semicircular entrance, with turrets of rusticated stone and brick.

moments.title: Jermyn
moments.text: In 1899, Dr. Matthew J. Shields taught 25 miners from the Jermyn Coal Colliery how to treat injured colleagues before a physician could reach the mine. The class met at the Windsor Hotel. Jermyn's early twentieth-century industries also included cut glass, silk, powder, sawmills and bottling works. The borough stands on the Lackawanna River and bears the name of John Jermyn, a mining businessman.

moments.title: Archbald Pothole
moments.text: The 38-foot-deep Archbald Pothole cuts through sandstone, shale and coal. Miner Patrick Mahon uncovered it in 1884 while extending a shaft. His blast released water and stones into the workings, and the miners fled. Almost 1,000 tons of rounded stones were removed before manager Edward Jones recognized the opening as a pothole. It first served as a mine ventilation shaft, then became a tourist attraction. The state park, on Business Route 6, formally opened in 1964. Glacial meltwater formed the hole; its elliptical opening narrows downward, from 42 by 24 feet to 17 by 14 feet at the bottom.
moments.notice: The pothole cuts through layers of sandstone, shale and coal.
